segments.say: Some conversations are hard because we know the other person well. Others are hard because they belong to a group that we've decided to distrust. Politics, religion, generations, ways of living. In these cases, we often arrive with a picture of the other side already in our heads. A growing body of research asks how accurate that picture is.

Social psychologists, notably Lee Ross at Stanford, described a common stance that they called naive realism. It has three parts. We believe that we see the world objectively, we believe that reasonable people will agree with us once they see the facts, and so we conclude that anyone who disagrees must be uninformed, irrational or biased.

show.sub: I see it as it is

segments.say: It's a stance that feels like plain common sense, which is why it's so hard to catch. Notice that each side in a disagreement holds it at the same time. Both think that they're the realist and the other is distorted by something.

show.title: The three beliefs of naive realism
items: I see things as they really are
Reasonable people see them the same way
Those who don't must be misinformed or biased

segments.say: Emily Pronin and her colleagues asked people how susceptible they were to a range of biases, such as the tendency to take credit for success and blame others for failure, compared with the average person. Most people said that they were less biased than the average person, which can't be true for most. And people didn't change their view even after learning about the bias.

show.what: The bias blind spot: perceptions of bias in self versus others

segments.say: The bias blind spot is a gentle name for a serious problem. It helps to explain why a conversation can go wrong even when both people have good intentions. Each person is quietly confident that the other one is the biased one, and so each sees little reason to adjust.

show.sub: The bias we can't see in ourselves

segments.say: If naive realism makes us assume that the other side sees things in a distorted way, how big do we think the gap is? And how big is it really? A line of research has tried to measure the difference between what people believe about the other side, and what the other side believes.

Douglas Ahler and Gaurav Sood surveyed Americans about the makeup of the two main parties. They found that people consistently overestimated how many members of the opposing party belonged to the groups that seemed most unlike them. People believed that the other side was more extreme and more stereotypical than it actually was, and when told the real numbers, their feelings towards the other party softened a little.

show.what: The parties in our heads: misperceptions about party composition and their consequences

segments.say: Other researchers have found a similar pattern. In several countries, people overestimate how extreme the other side's views are, and underestimate how much they share. A large survey project called the Perception Gap, led by the group More in Common, found that those who followed politics most closely were often the most mistaken about their opponents, though the details differ between surveys.

This is not a claim that there are no real differences. There are many, and some of them are deep. It's a claim that the distance is often smaller than it feels, and that part of the heat in a conversation comes from arguing with a version of the other person that doesn't quite exist.

show.title: What the perception gap research suggests
items: We imagine the other side as more extreme than it is
Those who are most engaged are not always most accurate
Correcting the picture can reduce hostility
The gap is bigger in our heads than in reality

segments.say: Why would we hold such an exaggerated picture? One answer is that we get our impressions of the other side from the loudest and most extreme examples. Moderate people are quiet. They don't go viral. So the people who represent a group in the news and on social media are often not typical of it at all.

show.title: Where do the stereotypes come from?

segments.say: The sociologist Chris Bail, whom we met in an earlier video, argued that social media creates a distorted mirror. Extreme voices post more and get more attention, while moderate people stay silent. The result is that we see the other side through its most outspoken members, and conclude that this is what they are like. It is a theory with support, though it's still being tested.

show.what: How to make our platforms less polarizing

segments.say: It follows that one of the best ways to reduce the distortion is to talk to ordinary people from the other side, face to face, about ordinary things. Not the person who shouts the loudest, but the one in the next office, the neighbour, the cousin. Such conversations tend to replace the cartoon with a person, and people are harder to dislike than cartoons.

There's another surprising finding. People often assume that the other side would not be interested in talking, or would be unpleasant if they did. But experiments show that such conversations are generally more pleasant than expected. In a series of studies, strangers who talked to each other, including across divides, enjoyed it more than they predicted.

Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder asked commuters in Chicago to either talk to a stranger on the train or bus, sit in silence, or do what they normally did. Those asked to talk reported a more positive commute, and productivity wasn't harmed. Yet before the task, most predicted that they would prefer solitude. The same pattern, expecting a conversation to be awkward and finding it enjoyable, has been repeated in many places.

Later work by Epley and others found that people also underestimate how much others enjoy being asked questions, being thanked, and being contacted out of the blue. The fear of an awkward conversation is usually larger than the reality. That doesn't mean every talk goes well. But it suggests that our first reaction, to avoid, is not the best guide.

Four terms from this chapter. Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it is. The bias blind spot is seeing bias in others and not in ourselves. The perception gap is the difference between what we think the other side believes and what it believes. And a stereotype is a simplified picture of a group.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter

segments.say: Here's a small experiment you can try this week. Think of one person whose views you find difficult. Write down, in a few sentences, what you think they believe and why. Then, if it's safe and possible, ask them. Don't argue, only ask, and listen to the answer. Many people find that their picture was partly right and partly a caricature. The distance between the two is the size of your own perception gap, and it's a good thing to know.

show.title: A small experiment
items: Think of someone you disagree with
Write down what you think they believe
Ask them what they actually believe

segments.say: Two sides of a table, and a lamp in the middle. The research on perception gaps suggests that the distance across that table is usually shorter than each side imagines, and that the light in the middle is closer to both of them than it looks.

Here are four signs that you may be arguing with a picture of the person, and not the person. First, if you can only describe their view in insulting words, it's probably not how they would describe it. Second, if you've never heard them state their position in their own voice, you may be relying on someone else's summary. Third, if you assume they hold every view that people in their group are supposed to hold, you're missing the individual. And fourth, if you'd be shocked to learn that you agree on anything at all, the odds are that you do, and haven't yet discovered it. None of this means they're right. It means that the argument you're having should be with them, not with a cartoon that is easier to beat.

show.title: Signs you may be arguing with a caricature
items: You can describe their view only in insulting terms
You've never heard them state it themselves
You assume they hold every view of their group
You'd be surprised if they agreed with you on anything

segments.say: There's a kindness in this research. It says that the person you're arguing with is probably less extreme, more complicated and more like you than the version in your head. That doesn't make their views right. But it means that you can disagree with a person, and not with a caricature, which is a far better place to begin.

show.sub: Real people are harder to hate

segments.say: So what did we learn? That each side thinks it sees the world as it is. That most people think they're less biased than average. That we imagine the other side as more extreme than it is. And that talking to a real person usually goes better than expected.
Next, we turn to the foundation of every good conversation: listening. What does it do to the person who's being listened to? The results are stronger than you might guess.
